name: Dynastes grantii
intro: With western Hercules beetles, I prepare more than one laying box before I pair the adults. A single female can produce a large number of eggs, and the grubs from one brood can reach pupation weeks apart. I keep the laying date with each box so I can follow the brood even after I move the adults.

sections.title: Adults
sections.text:
I offer active adults beetle jelly every five days, or apple or banana. I let a newly emerged beetle come up and start feeding before I introduce a mate. I keep the pair where I can see both beetles on the surface, with enough substrate below for the female to burrow. Once I have seen them pair, I can move the female to her own laying box. I like a clear-sided box because I can sometimes see eggs or a pupa without digging.
When planning for older adults, I keep in mind an unusually long-lived Arizona male documented by Krell and Krell. It survived nine months and one week after collection. That is a useful upper-end comparison when an active western Hercules beetle lives well beyond the breeding season.

sections.title: Eggs and larvae
sections.text:
One female gave me 87 eggs. In a different box that originally held more than 80 eggs, I later found just 12 living larvae. I keep those counts separate when planning how many rearing containers I need. A large egg count tells me how much space to prepare, but the number of feeding grubs can be quite different.
For growing rhinoceros beetle larvae I recommend thoroughly fermented hardwood flake soil. I use a more fermented batch than I would for stag beetles or jewel scarabs. I check the substrate while the larva is still feeding so I can replace exhausted food before it begins making a cell.

sections.title: Pupation
sections.text:
In one brood, a single grub reached the prepupal stage long before its siblings. In a display enclosure I could see a larva starting its pupal cell on September 23 and a pupa at the wall on October 17. I keep the cell intact and continue checking the slower grubs separately. When a chamber is visible through the side, I can follow the stages without lifting it out. I wait until a new adult comes out on its own and is feeding before I pair it.
In one earlier pair the male had already emerged while the female was still a pupa. She completed her adult molt the day I photographed the male. I keep each chamber intact even if its occupant appears to be behind the rest of the group.

sources.title: F.-T. Krell and V. H. I. Krell (2015). Longevity of the western Hercules beetle, Dynastes grantii Horn. The Coleopterists Bulletin 69, 760.

native_status.text: Native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. The documented range includes Arizona, New Mexico, Utah and Chihuahua.
